utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So good morning. Madam Registrar, could you call the case please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. All the accused are present. The Prosecution is Mr. McCloskey. Absent from the Defence teams are Mr. Lazarevic, Mr. Krgovic, Mr. Ostojic. That's it, I think. All right. Good morning to Mr. Haynes and Mr. Pandurevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We can start. We'll dispose of two matters of housekeeping very quickly. On the 15th of January, the Borovcanin Defence team filed the second motion for admission of 88 documents from the bar table. On the 29th of January, the Prosecution filed a response not objecting to the Defence motion. For this reason, and also because the reasons submitted in the motion themselves are acceptable, are good, the Trial Chamber hereby grants the motion. Now, on the 16th and on the 23rd of January, the Pandurevic Defence team filed their third and fourth motions respectively seeking leave to amend the Rule 65 ter list of exhibits. On the 30th of January, the Prosecution filed the combined response not objecting to the motions. The Trial Chamber, for these reasons, grants the motions. Incidentally, on the 29th of January, but we only got it later, in my case I only got it today, the Pandurevic Defence team filed their fifth motion seeking leave to amend their Rule 65 ter list of exhibits. I don't know, Mr. McCloskey, if you have had an opportunity to look at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I don't think I have but I don't imagine there will be any objection. But I will take a look at the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. Thank you. On your part, Mr. Haynes, if documents mentioned in the annex are amongst those that you will be using today, please draw our attention.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes, I'll do my best.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. And we'll try and solve it there and then as it arises.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. I think you can continue your direct, your examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you, and good morning to you. Good morning everybody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Mr. Pandurevic, on Friday afternoon when we finished off, you were telling us about events in the morning of the 15th of July at the forward command post at Krivace, and you had just told us about some documents that General Krstic had handed to you and that you had read. So that we've got a picture of it, was there a discussion going on between you and General Krstic as you read the documents or did he just leave you with the documents to read?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After having read the documents or, rather, having had a look at them, I assessed the situation very briefly and I addressed General Krstic whether a request to grant me to return to the zone of responsibility of the brigade where I was going to deal with the problems at hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And what was his response?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It took him a while to think about it. He was assessing the situation on the front line around Zepa, and he knew that the withdrawal of the tactical group and its pulling out of its direction of use would pose a problem for him because he would have to replace those forces and cover the area with some other men. And in that sense he was not very decisive. He was not in a position to make that decision immediately and send me to Zvornik right away. However, being -- confronting him with my request and the situation in the territory of Zvornik, his final decision was for me to return to Zvornik together with my forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I don't believe you told us this on Friday, so let's clear this up. About what time in the morning was it that you went to the forward command post?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that that was sometime around 9.00, maybe a few minutes before 9.00 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And how long were you there before General Krstic made his decision that you should return to Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's very hard for me to pinpoint the time. I can't give you anything in terms of minutes or hours. In any case, I spent as much time as I needed to look at the documents, carry out that conversation with General Krstic and after that, to also carry out certain conversations with the command of the Zvornik Brigade. It may have lasted some 15, 20 minutes, half an hour at the most altogether.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, thank you. You've answered my next question, which is: Did you speak to the command of the Zvornik Brigade that morning?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course. The reports in the documents that I had a look at were not enough for me to provide me with a complete insight into the situation that the documents referred to, and that's why I contacted the IKM of the corps and asked them to allow me to use their RU-1 radio relay device and to establish a connection with the command of the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Can we have a look please at P1171, A in the English and B in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: This is an intercepted radio communication at 8.34 on the morning of the 15th of July and I'm only concerned with the very small entry at the bottom of the page in B/C/S, Mr. Pandurevic. While you were at Krivace, did you come to know that Semso Muminovic wanted to talk to you?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that this was conveyed to me at the IKM. At this very moment, I don't remember that; however, in view of the significance of that information, I would be of the opinion that Mr. Jevdjevic did convey that message on to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: It probably doesn't matter and you may not recall, but do you recall whether that was before, during or after your reading of the documents and your discussion with General Krstic?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was probably after that because my first contact when I arrived at the IKM was my contact with General Krstic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Can we have a look at P1173, please. That's, I think, A in the B/C -- D in the English and A in the B/C/S, I think. No, D in both.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, when you made contact with the command of the Zvornik Brigade, who did you originally speak to?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, this could have been either Milosevic or Jokic was my first point of contact; however, you could establish that based on the analysis of these conversations and the information contained herein. It would be overly ambitious for me to try and reconstruct the sequence of the conversations. In any case, I spoke to Milosevic, Mijatovic, and Jokic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: What was your particular interest in speaking to Mijatovic?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was particularly interested in the situation in the area of responsibility of the brigade with regard to the documents that I had already read before. I knew that the most complex situation was to be expected in the western part of the defence zone, which was the defence sector of the 4th, 6th and the 7th Battalions, i.e., the positions ranging from Petkovci to Memici in the west. Since Mr. Mijatovic at one point in time was the battalion commander in Baljkovica and he was best -- most familiar with the terrain, he was the one who could provide me with the most accurate information with this regard.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And was he at the command Standard on the morning of the 15th when you called?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He must have been. I'm sure he was. I spoke to them. They used the same telephone because his office and Milosevic's office are two adjacent offices to the office of the duty operations officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: How did you leave things during the first conversation you had?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As you can see in this conversation, I inquired about the 4th, the 6th and the 7th Battalion. Milosevic provided me with certain information which was not completely consistent and he, himself, did not have enough information to be able to portray the situation or assess it in real time. However, information that I obtained during those conversations was more favourable than the information contained in the documents that I had perused.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: At the bottom of the intercept that we're looking at, it suggests that you told Mijatovic to call the 4th, 6th and 7th Battalion and report back to you; is that your recollection of how you left things?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I asked them to check the situation immediately. I wanted to have the situation in real time. I wanted to know at the moment when I was calling what the situation was on the front line. That's why I asked them to do that and I told them that I would call back, that I would talk to them again.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Can we now have in e-court, please, P1174, A in the English and B in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: This intercepted conversation is timed at 9.10 on the morning of the 15th of July, so if the timing is accurate, about 15 minutes after the conversation we were just looking at. Do you recall when you called back the second time speaking to Jokic?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When I called back the second time, Jokic was probably the duty operations officer. He replied. However, I did not talk to him about the situation at all. I knew him very well. I knew that he was a man who is faced by complicated situations and he is not able to convey the real picture of the events. That's why I wanted to be put through to Mijatovic immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And do the responses recorded as being made by Mijatovic in this intercept accord with your recollection of the conversation you had the second time you called the brigade?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was the information that Mijatovic had obtained after my initial conversation with him. In the meantime, he had spoken to the units on the lines, and since this is not a very legible handwritten version, but I remember that he said everything is okay on the lines, I think, and that a chief, and I believe that he meant Obrenovic, said there were long columns -- it's very hard for me to read everything that it says here. If you have a typewritten version, it would be better. In any case, this is the most recent information, an update that I received at that time, at 0910.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, just to give you the opportunity, I don't think it will advance things very far, but the typewritten version is 1174 D, so if you would just like to have a quick look at that to assure yourself that nothing has been missed by you. The document in e-court will need to be on page 2.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is it. The situation on the front line is good, stable. Parts of the 28th Division, according to an estimate, some 4.000 to 5.000 of them are encircled, and according to his information, Naser with a group has entered Krizevici. And this would be all that it says in this intercept.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, you were present at Zepa pursuant to an order. Did it require an order for your unit to pull out of Zepa?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since I had participated in Stupcanica 95 operation, the commander of that operation, General Krstic, had to issue a special order for my unit to be pulled out and sent to Zvornik. And as far as I can remember, he did issue a written order for that to be carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Can we have a look at 7D686, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: We'll have a look at this in a little detail. This is an order dated the 15th of July. If we go to the bottom, we can see the time at which it was sent; it appears to be 10.41. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I see at the end a handwritten note, "at 1000 hours" outside of the original square.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And in the body of the order, it says: "The Drina Corps Commander has decided to return part of the forces of the 1st Zvornik Infantry Brigade and the Podrinje Special Forces Detachment to their zones of responsibility where they are to take measures to remove and prevent the consequences of a possible attack on Zvornik and the link-up of Muslim units from Srebrenica and Tuzla." And then in the body of the order: "The 1st Zvornik Infantry Brigade, the Ministry of the Interior forces, and the attached units shall take all measures to block and, if possible, break up and capture Muslim forces until the arrival of parts of the Zvornik Infantry Brigade and the POSS." The first half of that order appears to relate to you. Are those the orders you understood General Krstic to be giving you in relation to the forces of the enemy that were in and around Zvornik at that time?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: The first paragraph under the heading "Order" appears to be addressed to somebody else. Who would that have been addressed to?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is "Return of the Elements of the 1st Zvornik Infantry Brigade." That's the title. And this was also sent to the command of the 1st Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: But I just was hoping to draw your comment on the fact that although the orders are very similar, one appears to be addressed to you and a separate one to Dragan Obrenovic, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, two separate tasks are contained in this order. The first one in the first part concerns the units that had been with me in Zepa and the other one concerns those units of the Zvornik Brigade which were in the zone of defence in Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Okay. Well, we'll leave that there. Just to tidy up the whole process of your discussion with General Krstic, the documents you were shown and the order you were given, were you shown any documents that made any reference to prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Did any part of the discussion you had with General Krstic concern prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, they didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And did you receive any order from General Krstic relating to prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Did you at the time you were at Krivace have any knowledge of the presence of prisoners of war in the Zvornik area?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't. I didn't know that there were prisoners of war anywhere. I didn't know that at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, what did you do following General Krstic's order?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Having received the order, I returned to the sector where my units were and I issued tasks to my subordinated officers. I ordered them to pull out the units from fighting to form a column, to organise a march and return to Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Was the removal of your units from the line a straightforward process?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since we were engaged in combat with the enemy, that was a very sensitive procedure, and removal from this combat engagement had to be carried out very carefully in order to avoid any losses. And we also did not want the enemy to conclude what our true intentions were. That is why the whole operation took a while.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: But once it had been achieved, what did you then do?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once the units were removed from combat engagement with the enemy and when I had issued my tasks to the officers, I was the one to leave with my escorts, my signalsmen, and I went in the direction of Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: About what time did you leave?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was sometime around 10.00 or maybe half past 10.00, or even closer to 11.00, thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Did you stop en route to Zvornik or did you go directly there?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember whether I stopped anywhere. I can't be sure of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And about what time did you get to Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I arrived in Zvornik around noon, around 1200 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, we'll just leave that to one side for a moment to have a brief look at the situation in the brigade that morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Could we have a look, please, at P377, the duty officer's notebook. I know Ms. Stewart's kindly brought the original with her again this morning, so if you can have a look at that, Mr. Pandurevic, you'll need to find the ERN number 5756. The rest of us can look at page 138 in the e-court version. 5756.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: It's the entry at the bottom of the page at 9.21. Obrenovic ordered an urgent request for reinforcements from the corps, reported. What can we glean from that as to your deputy's understanding at 9.21 in the morning?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The duty operations officer recorded Obrenovic's order for an urgent reinforcement from the corps, and it says underneath that Badem sent reinforcements, and I believe that Badem at the time was the code-name for the Bratunac Brigade. This is a sequence to Obrenovic's request that he sent in the interim combat report, sent from Zvornik at 0110 hours, between 14 and 15 July, as far as I can remember. I remember having seen that report at Krivace. He did not request for my return expressly, but he just requested for reinforcement to be sent.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now we can have a look at P1176; that's A in the English and B in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: This is a conversation intercepted and recorded as being at 9.39 on the morning of the 15th of July.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Haynes, the B/C/S version is under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Then it should not be broadcast.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: A conversation between Zlatar, which is what?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This intercept is a conversation between the duty officer of Palma and the one of Zlatar, that is, the Zvornik Brigade and the Drina Corps respectively.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And here we see the duty officer at Zlatar saying: "Z: Put me through to the duty officer. "P: Right away, hello. "Z: This is the Zlatar duty officer." And the duty officer at Zvornik: "P: Major Jokic, duty officer at Palma. "Z: Jokic. "P: Yes. "Z: Your /deserters?/ are coming to you. "P: Pardon? "Z: Your ... they are coming. "P: Who is coming?" says Major Jokic. "Z: Your lot, fuck it. "P: Our lot with the boss. "Z: Come on, stop blabbering, bye. "P: Bye." What does this intercepted conversation appear to record?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The duty officer of Zlatar tried to inform the duty officer of Palma in good time that the unit under my command was on its way back. He intended to do that briefly and in code so that whoever was listening in would not understand, but it turned out the other way. So whoever was listening was able to conclude what this was about. In any case, he is informing Jokic that the forces which had been at Zepa were on their way back.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, I think we can leave that there. Now, with whom did you travel from Zepa to Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, the driver, escort and communications man.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And when you arrived at Zvornik, was there anyone on the gate to the barracks?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was a policeman at the gate. I don't know if it ever happened that there was no policeman or soldier on duty at the gate controlling the entrance, people coming in and out. And the policeman opened the gate so that the vehicle could go in.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: What did you do when you arrived?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On entering the barracks, my vehicle always parked in front of the entrance to the building. And one member of the escort always went ahead of me, I would follow him, and another member of my escort would walk behind me. I immediately went up to the first floor where my office was and also the office of the Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Did you notice any other cars in the carpark Standard when you arrived?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. There were some parked cars, but I didn't know whose they were at that point in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Who did it turn out they belonged to?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I learned later on that these were cars belonging to Mr. Vasic and Mr. Borovcanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Once you got inside the building, did you see anybody?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In front of me was my escort, the soldier escorting me, and at the steps in front of the office of the operations duty officer, he stopped and I went on down the corridor towards my office. He remained where he was and went to another room. There was nobody else in the corridor at that point in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And which room did you go to first?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since my job was urgent, I went straight to the office of the Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And what did you do when you got to the office of the Chief of Staff?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I entered the office of the Chief of Staff, at the head of the table was Dragan Obrenovic. I remember Mr. Vasic, Borovcanin, Danilo Zoljic, and Miso Stupar. Whether there was anyone else, I can't recall now. Of all these people, with the exception of Borovcanin, I had seen them all before and I knew them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Were they standing up or sitting down?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Obrenovic was the only one who got up; the others remained sitting down. I said to Obrenovic, "Can you inform me immediately about the situation on the front?"

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And what did he do?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As there was a map hanging on the wall, he took a pointer and explained to me what the situation was in the area of defence of the brigade and what activities had taken place that morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Did he tell you what he knew about the size of the enemy force you were dealing with?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He gave me his assessment, that was his own assessment, and also the information he had received from intelligence which had been submitted to him by Captain Vukotic and our intercepts centre. And he told me that the forces of the 28th Division were in the area of Crni Vrh, Planinac, and that there were maybe 5.000 to 6.000 men in total, some armed and some unarmed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And what information was there as to where the forces of the 28th Division were headed?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The information he gave me was that the 28th Division intended to continue moving across Crni Vrh and Planinac and to come out at Nezuk. He said that from the early morning there had been attacks by parts of the 2nd Corps from the front but that the front line had not moved at any point. Our positions at the front end were stable. There was information that Naser Oric, with a group, had entered the village of Krizevici but that was not correct. That was only a ploy they used, trying to get us to believe that through the radio communications.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Given the state of the information you had at that meeting, were you concerned for the security of the town of Zvornik itself?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In view of the location of the 28th Division and the intentions we had assessed they had, I was fully aware that there was no threat to Zvornik, that the threat was over and that no one had the intention of attacking Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Why was that?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The forces of the 28th Division had only one goal and that was to reach the territory controlled by the 2nd Corps of the BH army, and their combat-readiness was such that they were unable to carry out any large-scale offensive activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Did the size of the force of the 28th Division worry you?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At any rate the numbers did play a role, but there was a bigger threat from the front line from the forces of the 2nd Corps. I knew, however, that in the column of the 28th Division -- rather, I assumed there were both armed and unarmed able-bodied men and that this column was marching -- rather, had been marching for some five days and that they must be exhausted.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: What did you -- what were your orders?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The orders I received from General Krstic were that I should stop the column, block it, prevent it from going further and destroy it, or rather to prevent them from joining up with the forces of the 2nd Corps. This same order was issued to the Zvornik Brigade. They were to do that until I returned. So acting on those orders, I issued tasks to the persons present in the office of the Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Just before we come on to the orders you issued, you've said that your orders were to destroy the column. What, in military terms, would that entail?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I said something about this the other day. "To destroy" means to carry out military activities which will destroy most of the enemy unit so that they no longer represent a military threat.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: What are the various ways in which that might be achieved?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's another term which is to neutralise. "To neutralise" means to render harmless in another way by disarming, imprisoning, capturing or putting the unit in a passive situation where it can no longer act.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: So if the 28th Division had laid down its arms and surrendered, that would have achieved destruction, would it, or neutralisation?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The division would have been neutralised or, rather, the military threat it represented would have been eliminated.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: In that event - I know it's a hypothetical question - did you have any idea what you might do with 5.000 to 6.000 prisoners?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would have been the first instance in all my military experience where there would be such a huge number of prisoners, and I would ask the corps for guidance as to what to do next.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. So let's move on to the tasks. What tasks did you issue to the people present at that meeting on the 15th of July?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As Obrenovic had told me in detail, the positions of the forces of the Zvornik Brigade, both those at the front line and those that had organised ambushes and roadblocks, Borovcanin told me about the state and disposition of his units. In compliance with the orders I had, I issued tasks that these units should be engaged in cutting off the forces of the 28th Division and defence from the forces of the 2nd Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: What was the overall plan of the tasks that you gave?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The overall plan was to strengthen the forward defence line or, rather, the positions of the 4th and 7th Battalions and prevent at any cost a break-through by the forces from the front, and then by cutting off the forces of the 28th Division, both from the flank and across, to neutralise the forces of the 28th Division.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Were you by the time of that meeting expecting other forces to join you?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew that at any moment a tactical group should arrive, the one that had been with me. I knew that in the area of Crni Vrh there were two companies previously engaged by Dragan Obrenovic. I knew that the Intervention Platoon of the 2nd Battalion was at Tisova Kosa, in that area, that is. And I knew that some other forces should arrive from Bratunac and some had already arrived and that the MUP units under the command of Ljubisa Borovcanin were ready to be used.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Did anybody at the meeting suggest any other course of action, other than strengthening the lines and cutting off the forces of the 28th Division?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were other suggestions. I think that Mr. Borovcanin put forward a suggestion that the forces of the 28th Division should be allowed to pass through, that the area should be opened up immediately for their free passage. There were other comments as to how to engage the forces of the VRS in carrying out the assigned task, but as there was a need for urgent action, I cut short the discussion. I reiterated the tasks I had issued and I said that everyone should now set out to implement those tasks. And if somebody did not wish to be engaged in this, they didn't have to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Why did you not feel able to entertain the suggestion that the forces of the 28th Division should be let to pass through at that stage?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had quite a lot of wartime experience as regards the information coming on the enemy coming in, and the information I trusted most was the information I obtained personally and convinced myself on the ground that it was true. It would have been irresponsible if the task I had been issued by General Krstic was changed by me in the office without my having gone out on the ground and seen for myself what the situation was. At that point in time I didn't want to accept any other suggestions.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: How long did the meeting last with you there?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The meeting didn't last long, at least not while I was there, only for as long as it took Obrenovic to explain the tactical situation, for us to have a brief discussion all together, for me to issue the tasks. So all this might have taken some 20 minutes or so. It's hard for me now to establish a time frame, but it wasn't long because I wanted to go to the forward command post as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And what happened at the end of the meeting?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the end of the meeting, I sent Obrenovic to the command of the 4th Battalion in Baljkovica, Borovcanin went to take his units to the Parlog and Baljkovica area, and I went to the forward command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, before we leave the command of the Zvornik Brigade, a few specific questions about the meeting and your arrival at the Standard barracks. Is there any truth in the suggestion that you saw Obrenovic on his own in the corridor before you went into his room?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Is there any question of Obrenovic stepping outside the room once you were all in the meeting together?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I entered the room and found them all inside. No one went out for the duration of the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And did anybody, Obrenovic or anybody else, mention during the course of that meeting anything about prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no one did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Just before the next series of questions, I'd like you to have a look at the notebook you have under your left arm again, please, and can you look at 5757. That's the ERN number of the page you need to see. For the rest of us, it's page 139 in the e-court version. And it's the entry right at the top of the page.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And it reads in the English: "The Turks have cut off the road to Crni Vrh, the Chief of Staff reported, 6th Infantry Battalion. IKM reports a column moving from Krizevici towards Motovska Kosa." Was the information about the cutting off of the road to Crni Vrh available to you before you set out from that meeting towards the IKM?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During his briefing on the overall situation on the ground, Obrenovic also conveyed information on the situation on the roads and the possibility of moving in certain directions, secure movement, and I knew that the road across Crni Vrh, Orahovac, and Krizevici was not safe.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: One of the routes to the forward command post would take you through Orahovac, wouldn't it? Did you go that way on the afternoon of the 15th of July?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the usual route one took to reach the 4th Battalion - Zvornik, Orahovac, Krizevici, Parlog, Baljkovica. But on that day I didn't take that route. I took the route Zvornik, Jardan, Cer, Kitovnice -- Jardan, Cer, Kitovnice. That was a safer and more secure route. The road was worse but it was safer.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Just to reinforce that point, can we have a look, please, at P2232, page 12; and 2231, that's the original page 16, and this is the book of tactical intercepts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Haynes, it's almost ten past 10.00. We stop at 20 past. Okay, I apologise to you. Yes, it's the second time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'll have to make these first sessions more interesting. You're obviously running out of patience with me 10 minutes before the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I raised it because you were going to start with a new thing, which I knew for sure you wouldn't finish in two minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: About two-thirds of the way down the page in the English, I don't know how easily you will identify it in the original script, Mr. Pandurevic, but there's an intercepted call between L-1 and Igman about the sending of 40 -- forces of 40 men. Can you see that? I don't know precisely where it is on the page in the -- thank you. It's exactly halfway down, right in the middle of the screen. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that L-1 is reporting to Igman-1 about the 40 men who should not be sent via Krizevici, and Krizevici is immediately about Orahovac, but rather to send them across Jardan, Kitovnice, and I can't read the last word.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The last word is Delici.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you find them in English? Could you take a look? It's page 16 in -- what we have in front of us is page 16. Is it the correct one?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Kwon. No, it's not. It should be page 12 in the English. Thank you very much, because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. I see it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes, it's two-thirds of the way down.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Mr. Pandurevic, in the original, did you say you can see the word "Jardan" before the Kitovnice?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Jardan is a village that you have to go through first in order to reach Kitovnice.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. I mean, even to my eye it's quite clear but it's recorded as "illegible" in the English translation but thank you for that. Was that the advice you'd received as to which route to travel towards the IKM, which of course is at Delici, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Can we deal with the forward command post. I think a long time ago now, the Trial Chamber and some of the lawyers in the case may have visited it, but in July of 1995 what would you actually have found at the forward command post at Delici in physical terms?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In very general terms, a forward command post is a room on the ground from which a commander with his command group oversees combat on the ground and commands this. During the war, the Zvornik command had three locations for IKMs. One IKM, in July 1995 and even before that, was in the village of Kitovnice, i.e., in the hamlet of Delici. In some of the maps you will see it referred to as Hajdukovici; however, this IKM in contrast, in physical terms, was a small prefabricated building with maybe two or three rooms which housed the communications centre, and next it was a container which housed the security and the signalsmen, and north of the object, some 300 metres away from it, was there was an observation point. It was a facility made of wood and earth and it was connected with wire with the prefabricated building. When I was in command at the IKM, I would always be at the observation point.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And was that where you were throughout the 15th of July?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As soon as I arrived in the Delici sector, I went to the observation post from which I had an opportunity to observe the entire area of combat.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And from there would you have been aware of everybody who came and went to and from the main building of the forward command post?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not know and I couldn't see the comings to and goings from the prefabricated building. As I've told you, I was 300 metres further away at the observation post, which was a dug-out building in the ground with two openings from which you could indeed observe what was going on, but it was also at the same time protected from artillery fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: What time did you arrive at the forward command post on the 15th?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 1300 hours would be that time, but it was actually sometime after 1300 hours, to the best of my recollection.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And at that time how did the situation on the ground appear to be to you?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The situation on the ground appeared completely different than described in my previous documents. In the defence sectors of the 4th and 6th Battalions, the situation was calm; there was no combat going on. On the left flank in the Memici sector, I could hear sporadic fire coming from there. The forces of the 28th Division, which were encircled, did not make any sound. So I can say that during that period of time, at the moment when I arrived at the IKM and the observation post, the situation was completely stable.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Can we have a look, please, at the next page in the book you have in front of us, 5759, and for the rest of us, B/C/S and English, page 141 in P377, the duty officer's notebook.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: General Pandurevic, I want to direct your attention to the entry at 1330 hours, which, according to your evidence, is about the time you first arrived at the forward command post, which reads: "Lazo reported that everything is okay at his end. The men from Bratunac have arrived and they are deployed at Parlog." Who is Lazo and what is he reporting on?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On this page, at 1330 hours, it says literally: "Lazo reports that everything is okay at his end. The men from Bratunac arrived and have been deployed in Parlog." This is information reported by the then Deputy Commander of the 4th Battalion, Lazar Ristic, who was in command of the 4th Battalion, while his commander Pero Vidikovic was in training in Banja Luka. This man, Lazar, appeared before this Trial Chamber as a witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Can we go on another page, please, in the duty officer's notebook; 5760 for you, Mr. Pandurevic, and for the rest of us, page 142.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: It's the big entry in the middle of the page, which reads: "A large group of armed and unarmed Turks is blocked in the wider area of Potocani. One should expect that at any given time this group shall attempt to break through in a stampede towards Nezuk. They say they can't do anything about it until the forces from the front do something. One should expect an attack from the front early in the morning. At 400 hours wake up all the troops with guns in their hands and boots on their feet." This is recorded in the duty officer's notebook during the afternoon of the 15th of July. Who is this a message from?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that this was entered in the late afternoon hours on the 15th. Based on my observation of the situation on the ground and information received from our surveillance sector and the reports of the battalion commanders and commanders of the units which were immediately involved in blocking the 28th Division, I received this type of information. I conveyed this information to the duty operations officer for him to be able to report to all the other battalions in the entire area of defence of the brigade. I wanted us to be prepared for possible combat engagement.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Where we see in the middle of that paragraph, "They say they can't do anything anything about it until the forces from the front do something ..." what sort of surveillance does that reveal that you had?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our radio surveillance station monitored the communication between the forces of the 28th Division and elements of the corps, and they became privy to the information that the 28th Division informed the corps that they could not do anything and that their destiny was in the hands of the 2nd Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. And did you, during the afternoon of the 15th of July, prepare yourselves for an attack in the early morning of the 16th?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection as to leading. He's putting times in. We have not established any time for this and so I think it's appropriate that the witness be asked to give times.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Times for what?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The reference we just have in the duty officer's notebook has no time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: He said, "... late afternoon, the 15th of July." Check the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, if we could get that from the witness clearly, then ...

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, we've got it from the witness but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: What time does this entry appear in the book, Mr. Pandurevic?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this diary on the previous page, we have the last recording at 1510. The following page does not contain any indications of time; however, given the contents of the message, i.e., the order which says that all the soldiers should be awake at 4.00 in the morning and prepared, this would mean that this was recorded late in the afternoon or at dusk even, because after that the handwriting in the logbook appears to have changed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And what preparations were you initiating by passing this message back?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Up to that time, all the forces of the Zvornik Brigade which were engaged in the general area of Baljkovica were in their positions. The forces of the 6th, 4th and the 7th Battalions had been reinforced and brought up to strength. The Borinski [phoen] Special Detachment had already been deployed partly in Tisova Kosa and partly closer to the command of the 4th Battalion. In the same sector there was also the Intervention Platoon from the 2nd Battalion. The tank company or, rather, two-thirds of it were deployed in the area of Sapari [phoen], prepared for engagement against the 7th Battalion, and part of the company was on the Krizevici-Parlog-Baljkovica axis. Two companies under the command of Milan Maric and Zoran Jovanovic respectively were deployed in the territory of Crni Vrh. The company from the Bratunac Brigade, behind the command post of the 4th Battalion, MUP units were deployed on the Baljkovica-Parlog axis, and as far as I can remember the police from the East Bosnia Corps were deployed at the contact line between the 4th and the 6th Battalions. Also, the mixed artillery division was prepared for use. This means that all the forces of the Zvornik Brigade were in full combat-readiness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We need to stop here.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: One last question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We need to stop here.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we'll continue in 25 minutes' time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: For the record, I just want to announce that we have received the filing from the Defence team for General Miletic announcing that he will not be with us tomorrow and that he will be waiving his right to be present. Let's proceed. Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I have no objections to the Pandurevic documents. I've informed Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So the motion of the 29th of January to which -- the Pandurevic motion of the 29th of January to which I referred to earlier is hereby being granted. Thank you. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Can we just have a look, please, again at the duty officer's notebook. It's a page before the large passage you were just looking at, so it's 5759 for you, Mr. Pandurevic; page 141 for us. It's the entry at 1512 which reads: "Premier reported that the enemy is getting closer to our lines. All units informed." We've heard a lot of evidence about it in this case, but just remind us what is Premier and what does this entry in the duty officer's notebook reflect?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I joined the Zvornik Brigade, I encountered this name, "Premier." This was the code-name for the radio surveillance centre of the Zvornik Brigade and it kept that code-name throughout the war. That radio surveillance centre intercepted successfully the enemy's radio communication throughout the war. This is one of the notes reflecting their activities in monitoring the communication of the 2nd Corps and provided timely information about the activities of the enemy.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. And just to complete what you've been telling us about your observations of the situation on the ground on the afternoon of the 15th of July, what did you expect the enemy to do?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I expected that the forces of the 2nd Corps would launch an offensive in order to take over the front line of the Zvornik Brigade and link up with the forces of the 28th Division. On the other hand, given the fact that the commander of the Muslim side, Semso Muminovic, had requested to talk to me and had left a frequency that could be used for that conversation, this was an additional argument for me to think that he had something to offer and that the situation could be resolved even without fighting.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: When did you first meet Semso Muminovic?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that this was sometime in late 1993. That's when our first personal encounter took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Can we have a look, please, at 7D454.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: This is a document dated the 11th of November, 1993, and entitled, "Negotiations Between the Zvornik Infantry Brigade Commander Major Vinko Pandurevic and the 106th Muslim Brigade Commander Semso Muminovic," and it reads: "At the initiative of the enemy, our commander, Major Vinko Pandurevic, met with the commander of the 106th Muslim Brigade, Semso Muminovic, at 1200 hours on the 8th of November, 1993, in the area between Pecina and Kovacevici. Apart from the commander, the following officers from our side attended the meeting: The Chief for Intelligence and Security Affairs, Second Lieutenant Dragan Nikolic; and Lieutenant Vitomir Tomic of the National Security. The talks focused on a prisoner exchange and establishing a cease-fire and a truce between the two brigades. The talks were constructive and showed mutual respect. It was agreed that the cease-fire and truce between the brigades would enter into effect at 1200 hours on the 10th of November of 1993." This is a document, if we go to the third page in English, the last page in both documents, please, this is one of those documents that is produced by your assistant commander for moral guidance, religious and legal affairs; is that correct? But, in fact, we can see that this event made its way into a regular combat report, if we now look at 7D945, the regular combat report for the 8th of November, 1993. Under the second paragraph of this document, does this refer to precisely the same meeting between you and Semso Muminovic?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it refers to the same event, the same meeting. This is a regular combat report where the corps command is being briefed as part of the regular report, and what we saw previously was information drawn up by the assistant for morale, religious and legal matters, Mr. Simic. In addition to this event, it encompasses a number of other pieces of information and is used for internal purposes within the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: What circumstances gave rise to the meeting between you on the 8th of November, 1993?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall all the details. I know where the meeting was held. This was between the confrontation lines on no-man's land, so to speak, and the topic was the one mentioned in the information. In view of the fact that the front line stretched between the Muslim forces of the Zvornik Brigade, which were right next to villages and farm land which had to be plowed and sown and harvested, the aim of both sides was to enable farm work to be carried out, depending on the season, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And what was the result of the meeting in November 1993?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The result was that we carried out an exchange. I think that a soldier was exchanged on that day or the next day, I'm not sure. We established a hotline and had mutual contacts, and in spite of the fact that in our regular combat report we included this information, I later received from the corps command a request addressed personally to me that I should send detailed information about this because the Main Staff was asking what kind of meeting this had been and why it had been held.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: After this, did you use the hotline?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did have occasional contact by radio, depending on the needs that I have just mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And what, generally, did you talk about when you spoke over the radio?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We spoke about respecting our previous agreements, although there was always a certain amount of suspicion that the other side might take advantage of the agreement to carry out a covert offensive activity. However, the experience was that the agreements were in fact complied with.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, going back to the 15th of July of 1995, you've told us a little bit about the intercepted communication we saw earlier in the morning involving Milenko Jevdjevic and the name Semso Muminovic. Did you become aware that he wanted to contact you when you got to the forward command post of the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the forward command post, Mica Petkovic gave me this same information. He was a desk officer in the intelligence organ. He said that Semso had asked to speak to me and had left a frequency on which we could communicate through the radio equipment, the KT Motorola that has been talked about so much here, something resembling a mobile phone.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And did you call him or did he call you?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the afternoon of the 15th, I called him. I contacted him.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: What inspired you to do that?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wanted to hear why he had been looking for me. I assumed he thought I was the most suitable person for him to talk to in connection with his requests.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: What did you imagine he wanted to talk to you about?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In any case, I thought that he wanted to talk about the column of the 28th Division.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: When did you first call him?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't tell you the exact time, but it was after the consolidation of the deployment of the units that I have just described. The situation was completely quiet at the time. It was in the afternoon. It was certainly after 1500 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: What did he say when you called him?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said that he had been trying to contact me before, that he wanted to talk to Obrenovic but that Obrenovic did not want to accept his offer, and he asked me to let the whole column of the 28th Division pass through in the area of Nezuk.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And during that first conversation, how did you respond to that?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that we could discuss that, that to the best of my knowledge, there were many civilians and unarmed men in the column and that I was willing to let that sort of people go to the free territory right away, but that those who were armed had to give themselves up.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And what did he say?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said that he was not interested in civilians, that he was interested in the armed part of the column of the 28th Division and that he would not accept my offer.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: When you said that the armed men had to give themselves up, did you mean they had to surrender as prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my original offer, yes, that was what I meant. However, when he said that he was not interested in civilians, I thought that he wanted to place the fate of the civilians on my shoulders and that he was fighting or struggling to preserve exclusively the 28th Division, and this prompted me to call him again.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: How long after the first call?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not long after, I called him again and suggested to him that he should designate a place for the civilians to gather so that they could pass through, because he was in communication with the column; that those who were armed should lay down their weapons and that then they, too, could leave, but that they could not pass through carrying weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And what was his response to that?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He continued insisting on his position and that was the end of our conversation at that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: So it's probably obvious but just articulate it for us, will you? What was the change in your position during the second conversation?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I considered the order I had been issued by the corps command. I also considered the meeting I had had in the command, in the office of the Chief of Staff. I considered the request of the commander of the opposite side and I thought I could carry out my task by neutralising the 28th Division by allowing it to pass on to the free territory without carrying any weapons with them, by making them lay down their arms.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, I want you to listen to something for us, please. This is the tape recording of a conversation, the surrogate sheet for which -- on which we'll all be able to read the words and the translation is 7D656. It's already an exhibit in the case. It was tendered through PW168. So would you just listen to this with us for a minute, Mr. Pandurevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is there a transcript available of this conversation?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes. It's 7D656 and it's on your screen now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I don't know whether you'd like to hear the piece again so that you can follow. We'll do that. That's probably better. It's actually quite easy to follow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think it will be better, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: It appears that the image on e-court stops the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, exactly. Let me just consult with my colleagues that it's okay that we can proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: We could give you a hard copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's okay. We can see it on the monitor. Can we proceed? We can proceed. We don't need to hear it again.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thanks very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Who is speaking on the intercepted conversation we've just heard?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Semso Muminovic and I.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And on what date was the conversation taking place that we've just listened to?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 15th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: In total on the 15th of July - we'll come to the 16th in due course - but in total on the 15th of July, how many times did you speak to Semso Muminovic on the radio?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's hard for me to remember now which conversation was when, but I think it was five or six, although I've seen Semso's statement to the effect that it was much more. But this is what I remember. This is my recollection.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And given the position you appear to have adopted in this conversation, can you help us as to which conversation we're listening to here - the first, the second, the third, the fourth, or fifth, or sixth?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think this is the third conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: What authority did you have to enter into these conversations with Semso Muminovic?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The authority -- well, I did not have specific authority from the superior command. Based on my own conscience, I assessed that it was a good idea for me to carry out this kind of conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: At the time -- well, I'll take a step back from that. Over what period of time on the 15th of July did you have these conversations?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you can't have this sort of conversation very often because the terrain is not flat and the communications equipment did not have a long range. So it wasn't easy to establish contact. This was after 1500 hours and before dark fell, so it was in the course of the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Were any of the conversations after dark fell?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not on the 15th -- sorry, no, no, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And during the time that you were engaged in these conversations, how did it appear to you the military situation was? Sorry, that's a very inelegant question. While you were talking to him, how did you view the military situation?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I engaged in negotiations only after I had stabilized the situation and deployed all the forces that would be needed if it came to a fight.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: So why in those circumstances were you prepared, on the 15th of July, to make an offer to allow the whole of the 28th Division to walk free to Nezuk?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The reasons were very rational. I would have been able to carry out the task in this way while saving many lives, or I could carry out the task using fire-power. I opted for this version, this possibility, and I knew that Semso knew well that the greater the pressure of his forces from the front line, the more fierce would be my firing on the blocked forces of the 28th Division, and that this was what led him to ask for a conversation with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Were agreements for cease-fire and the safe passage of enemy soldiers tactics you'd ever deployed in the past?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As is well-known here, I had done similar things before. I considered the use of force and weapons to be something that should be done only in the direst necessity. It was only a last resort.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, throughout the afternoon of the 15th of July, who was present with you at the forward command post or observation post?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection, when I arrived at the forward command post, I found the signalsmen there; two or three, I don't know how many. I think Mica Petkovic was there, whom I have mentioned from the intelligence organ. The Chief of Communications, Captain Milisav Petrovic, arrived together with me. After a while, the President of the Municipal Council of the Serbian Democratic Party, Brano Grujic, paid a brief visit subsequently, and in the afternoon Ljubo Bojanovic arrived. There may have been someone else, but I don't recall that now.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I just want to leave that there for a minute because I want you to clear up something that appears ambiguous in the transcript. When you said earlier that you would have been able to carry out your task in this way while saving many lives, "... or I could carry out the task using fire-power. I opted for this version..." what were you saying you did?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the version of negotiations and agreements.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, can we just have a look, please, at a page in the duty officer's notebook. For us on e-court it's page 92, and the page you want to look at, Mr. Pandurevic, ends 710. And if you would just look at the very top entry, it's just the name at 1400 hours, "Brano Grujic." Is that the man you're referring to as having been present at the forward command post on the 15th of July?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's the man. He used to be the president of the municipality, but in 1995 he was only the president of the party. He was a man I was not on good terms with from the moment of my arrival in Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Did any of the people present at the forward command post on the afternoon of the 15th of July tell you anything about prisoners in schools in the Zvornik area?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only Brano Grujic did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And at what time was he at the forward command post and for how long?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's really hard for me to tell you the precise time of his arrival. I knew it was after my arrival, maybe an hour or an hour and a half later. He didn't stay long. He simply arrived and asked me how come there were prisoners in some schools on the territory of Zvornik municipality. I think he mentioned the school in Petkovci and the one in Pilica.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: What information did you get from what he told you or asked you?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said that his party activists in the local communes had conveyed this information to him and that there was concern in the local community where these people were situated. I said I did not have any specific information about this and that I would check to see what it was all about. He continued asking me questions about the situation on the ground, because his native village was Baljkovica, and then he left.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Did you check?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The persons who were then at the forward command post were persons who were unable to provide me with any information. When Ljubo Bojanovic arrived, and he was from the brigade command, in the operations organs sometimes and sometimes in the organ for morale, I asked him to give me more detailed information concerning what Mr. Grujic had told me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And what did Ljubo Bojanovic tell you?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ljubo Bojanovic told me that he knew that some buses with prisoners had passed by the command and that they had gone in the direction of Bijeljina. But whether they stopped in some schools in the Zvornik area or not, he didn't know, so he said. And he said he didn't know that the command of the Zvornik Brigade had received any task concerning prisoners of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Was he the only other person that you spoke to?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On that day, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, I appreciate it's difficult, I'm sure we all do, but approximately what time did you speak to Ljubo Bojanovic?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't mind answering any question; however, it is rather difficult to pinpoint times, as you say. But I believe that the conversation with Ljubo Bojanovic took place maybe an hour before I drafted the interim combat report for that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: What about your deputy Obrenovic? Didn't you check with him on the 15th?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time Obrenovic was in Baljkovica at the command of the 4th Battalion, so I did not discuss that matter with him on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, in general terms, what circumstances would lead you to send an interim combat report to corps command?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since General Krstic had sent me to Zvornik in the first place, there would be one important reason which was the aggravation of the tactical and combat situation. That's why I believed that it was my duty to draft an interim combat report and report to the corps command about the combat situation in the zone of defence of the Zvornik Brigade. Any other officer would have done the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Before you sent your report on the 15th of July, what was your understanding as to the state of the corps' information as to the size and motives of the column of the 28th Division?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was my impression that the corps command did not have all the necessary information about the size and the intentions of the 28th Division. Obrenovic had hinted to the fact at the meeting on the 15th, because his previous report that he had sent to the corps command, at least according to what he believed, had not been taken seriously. And I believed that once I received complete information about the 28th Division, that I should put all that information in an interim combat report.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, how was the interim combat report of the 15th of July made?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally dictated to Mr. Bojanovic at the observation point, so I dictated the report to Mr. Bojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And what did he do?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was dictating and he was writing in his own hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And did he read it back to you or did you read over what he had written?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He did not read it back; I did not read it. I just initialled the report and it was sent to Zvornik at the communications centre there, where it would be encrypted and sent to the corps command.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And how was it sent to Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A courier driver took it there by car. In any case, it could not have been encrypted and sent in an encrypted form from the IKM.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Give us some idea of the mood you were in at the time you dictated that report to Ljubo Bojanovic?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was tired. I had been on the ground for 12 days, did not get enough sleep. I worked hard. Second of all, all the proposals that I had sent to the corps command and the command of the Main Staff with regard to the measures that should be taken in respect of the 28th Division had been rejected, and for that reason I was disappointed, even angry. However, I did draft the report and I did it based on the situation and the information that I was privy to at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Then let's look at it. P329, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please could I be provided with a hard copy?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: The first paragraph reads: "Since the fall of Srebrenica, in the territory of the 1st Zvornik Infantry Brigade area of responsibility, in the wider area of Pandurice, Planici, Crni Vrh, Kamenica, and Glodjansko Brdo, there are about 3.000 armed and unarmed enemy soldiers. Brigade forces are sealing off and searching the aforementioned region. A few hundred enemy soldiers have so far been liquidated." Where did you get the information which you set out in paragraph 1 of that report?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I received this information mostly from Dragan Obrenovic at a meeting in his office. Some of the information I received from my subordinate commanders on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: As to the number of enemy soldiers in the area, did Obrenovic tell you there were 3.000 or a different figure?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The figure he gave me was a bit higher and I subsequently reduced it somewhat.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Why did you do that?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if you follow the part of this report to its end, the previous paragraphs follow a certain logic and tally with how the report ends. I knew what my final intentions were in terms of the accomplishment of the mission given to me by General Krstic. The information that several hundreds of enemy soldiers had been killed by then was rather arbitrary.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, you've pre-empted the question. What does the word "liquidated" mean in this report?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a classical military term which is used in order to show losses in fighting.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And did you have any information that a few hundred enemy soldiers had been killed in fighting during the 15th of July?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew that they did suffer losses, but it was unlikely that there were a few hundred killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Can we go to the second paragraph: "Throughout the 15th of July, BH army forces of the Tuzla 2nd Corps launched fierce attacks on the brigade defence area in order to link up with the forces which had been cut off. The attack on the defence area of the 4th, 6th and 7th Battalions along the Petkovci-Memici stretch was launched at 4.30 with simultaneous actions by the besieged forces." Where did this information come from?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This information was obtained from Dragan Obrenovic and battalion commanders. At the time, at 4.30 in the morning, the blocked forces were in Snagovo and Crni Vrh. That's where most of their activities were taking place. They did not move anywhere forward from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: The reference in that paragraph to fierce attacks on the brigade defence area, was that an accurate reflection of the situation on the ground on the 15th of July?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as artillery is concerned, yes, but as far as infantry assaults are concerned, the answer would be no. There were some attempts, but they failed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: The artillery attack that's reported as starting at 4.30 in the morning, when, to your knowledge, did that finish?
